issues.quote: FPSC's classic format here is direct voice conversion — "change the voice" given a full active or passive sentence to rewrite, not just spot-the-error — so you must reproduce the exact auxiliary for the tense, not merely recognise it. The examiner's favourite trap is an intransitive verb (occur, happen, arrive, consist) dressed up in a passive-sounding sentence, which has no correct passive at all: the only "correction" is to leave it active.
issues.explanation: Claims about FPSC formats, favourite traps, frequency or examiner preferences have no source identifiers or authentic-paper evidence in this lesson. These are not verified by a grammar authority.
issues.proposed_correction: Remove frequency/preference guarantees; describe the newly authored practice formats. Retain examination-specific claims only after recording authentic paper/year/item evidence.

issues.quote: Reported speech dominates the "Narration" section as full-sentence conversion questions, not spot-the-error — you are given direct speech in quotation marks and four candidate reported versions. The reliable trap is an option that gets the tense backshift exactly right but leaves a pronoun, or here/tomorrow, unconverted, or the reverse: correct time words riding on the wrong tense, banking on candidates checking only the verb.

issues.quote: Articles are tested as a two-blank fill-in-the-blank item across one sentence, and as error-spotting with four underlined parts where one article is wrong (a genuine "no error" option is sometimes present). The favourite trap pairs a correct sound-based a/an choice with a wrong "the" before a general abstract noun, so a candidate who checks only the article they were already suspicious of waves the whole sentence through.

issues.quote: Pronoun questions are set as error-spotting (four underlined parts, one a wrong form or a mismatched antecedent) and as full-sentence rewrites that force you to remove an ambiguous reference by naming the noun again. The trap is a decoy: examiners underline "and I" or "their" in a spot that already sounds fluent, so a candidate trusting their ear over the delete-the-other-person or singular-antecedent test picks the natural-sounding wrong option.

issues.quote: Modifier questions are almost always error-spotting, and the underlined part is often not the misplaced word itself but a neighbouring phrase, forcing the candidate to notice that the true fault is a word's position rather than any single word's form. The trap is a dangling participle in an otherwise flawless sentence, so a candidate scanning for verb or article mistakes sails straight past it.

issues.quote: Prepositions are tested as a pure fill-in-the-blank vocabulary item on one fixed collocation, or as error-spotting where a wrong preposition is grafted onto an otherwise flawless sentence. The favourite trap is a verb that takes no preposition in English at all but does under Urdu influence (discuss about, request for, reach at) — it sounds natural precisely because the Urdu equivalent needs that word, which is why intuition fails here more than anywhere else in the course.

issues.quote: This topic is tested with fill-in-the-blank items offering four verb forms (bare infinitive, to-infinitive, gerund, past participle) for one blank, and with error-spotting where the wrong non-finite form follows a verb that looks similar to one taking the opposite pattern. The sharpest trap pairs two near-synonyms that take different forms in the same sentence, so fixing the one fault you notice first can make you assume the sentence is now correct and miss the second.

issues.quote: Comparison faults appear as error-spotting where the flawed sentence sounds perfectly smooth (a rate or salary compared directly with a place name), and as rewrite items in the mixed-precision section that stack a comparison fault with an agreement or preposition fault from an earlier day. The favourite trap is a double comparative hidden inside a form that already looks irregular (more worse, most best), because a candidate checking the comparison logic assumes an odd-looking irregular form is already above suspicion.

issues.proposed_correction: Remove frequency/preference guarantees; describe the newly authored practice formats. Retain examination-specific claims only after recording authentic paper/year/item evidence.

issues.quote: CSS/FPSC papers test connectors mainly through underlined error-spotting items (four segments, sometimes with a "no error" option) and through fill-in-the-blank items that force a choice between a conjunction, a conjunctive adverb and a prepositional phrase for the same logic. The commonest trap is a decoy that looks fine read aloud — doubled connectors like "although … but", or despite followed by of — because the ear accepts what the eye should reject. A second trap plants a grammatically correct but logically wrong connector, such as therefore where the sentence actually concedes a point, testing whether you read for meaning and not just structure.

issues.quote: Parallelism is examined almost entirely through "which sentence is correct/parallel" MCQs and underlined error-spotting on lists of three or more items, rarely through a direct rule question. The standard trap hides the broken item third in a list, after two correctly matched items have already lulled the reader into accepting the pattern. A second trap swaps only the preposition or auxiliary partway through a correlative pair such as not only … but also, so the sentence still sounds balanced unless you isolate each half and test it alone.

issues.quote: The subject performs the action / The subject receives the action
issues.explanation: Active/passive are grammatical voice relations, not invariably doer/receiver meanings; know, have and psychological verbs show why semantic labels alone are inadequate.
issues.proposed_correction: Define active as the unmarked voice pattern; define passive through corresponding object/subject alignment and passive verb form. Use agent/patient as common interpretations, with exceptions.

issues.quote: Only transitive verbs can be made passive.
issues.explanation: Prepositional passives exist: a car can be broken into; a proposal can be objected to. The bare verb need not take a direct object in the active.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach ordinary direct-object passives plus lexical restrictions and prepositional passives; restrict no-passive advice to the relevant verb use.

issues.quote: He wants to sign the order. → He wants the order to be signed.
issues.explanation: The active identifies him as the prospective signer; the model passive allows someone else to sign. This is not a meaning-preserving voice transformation.
issues.proposed_correction: Use He wants to sign the order → He wants the order to be signed by him, explain awkwardness, and contrast the different control interpretation without the agent. Prefer a clearer finite-clause transformation for beginners.

issues.quote: A few verbs have both uses: The prices rose. / The government raised the prices.
issues.explanation: Rise and raise are different lexemes; this pair does not exemplify one verb with transitive and intransitive uses.
issues.proposed_correction: Use The door opened / Mina opened the door for an alternation; teach rise/raise separately as a lexical contrast.

issues.quote: A verb with two objects yields two possible passives
issues.explanation: Ditransitive constructions have lexical and regional restrictions; two objects do not guarantee both passive subjects or both passives as natural alternatives.
issues.proposed_correction: Qualify the generalisation with many verbs such as give/send, then teach lexical restrictions and naturalness.

issues.quote: The test ... is whether the subject arranged, paid for or caused the action
issues.explanation: The same have + object + participle pattern can express an adverse experience rather than arranged causation, as the lesson itself notes for wallet theft.
issues.proposed_correction: Separate causative and experiential readings; do not use deliberate arrangement as a universal diagnostic.

issues.quote: It is believed by many people that the scheme has failed.
issues.explanation: The sentence labelled wrong is grammatical; the proposed active rewrite is a stylistic choice. The c5 passive also need not be erroneous and will backshift is context-sensitive.
issues.proposed_correction: Label as valid alternatives and ask which best serves an explicitly supplied discourse context. Keep grammar scoring separate from style.

issues.quote: The draft policy has circulated to all provincial departments for comment.
issues.explanation: Circulate has intransitive and transitive uses; the draft can circulate. The explanation incorrectly assumes an active subject must circulate some other object.
issues.proposed_correction: Replace with an unambiguously transitive-only verb, e.g. The draft policy has distributed to all departments, or add no error and explain the valid intransitive reading.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: By whom the decision was taken remains unclear.
issues.explanation: By whom the decision was taken is an embedded interrogative subject of remains unclear. It correctly has uninverted order. The key treats it as a direct question despite its matrix predicate.
issues.proposed_correction: Include a no-error answer or replace with direct question By whom the decision was taken? and key the missing inversion.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: Occur and collapse are intransitive and have no passive forms.
issues.explanation: Collapse also has transitive senses, including folding an object. The correction is suitable for the earthquake context, but its lexical universal is false.
issues.proposed_correction: Say collapse is intransitive in the intended houses-fell-down reading; contrast transitive folding/demolition uses.

issues.quote: believe is stative and does not take the continuous
issues.explanation: Stative interpretations usually resist ordinary progressives, but lexical categorisation is not a complete impossibility claim. Here the impersonal passive needs is believed regardless of broader dynamic uses.
issues.proposed_correction: Explain the actual passive complement pattern and qualify stative progressive restrictions; avoid an unrestricted ban.

issues.quote: Change all four, or the sentence will be half-reported.
issues.explanation: Pronouns, demonstratives and time/place expressions change only where referents or temporal/spatial viewpoint require it. Same-place/same-day reporting may retain here/today/tomorrow. Modal shifts also depend on meaning.
issues.proposed_correction: Give the reporting context before transformation; teach optional tense shifts and referent-preserving pronoun/deictic choices.

issues.quote: Tell needs a person straight after it ... grammatically incomplete without naming who was addressed
issues.explanation: This holds for the illustrated tell + that-clause pattern, not every tell construction: tell a story, tell the truth, tell a lie and tell the difference need no recipient.
issues.proposed_correction: State the pattern-specific constraint and give major lexical exceptions; avoid deriving valency from the communicative meaning alone.

issues.quote: no do/does/did ... Delete do, does and did
issues.explanation: Positive interrogative do-support disappears when embedding, but negative auxiliaries and emphatic do may remain: He asked why she did not attend.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach removal of positive interrogative inversion/do-support, retain negation and emphatic meaning where appropriate.

issues.quote: A question tag ... follows the same rule
issues.explanation: An ordinary tag is not an embedded interrogative and retains its question structure: The file is ready, is it not?
issues.proposed_correction: Separate tag formation from embedded clause order. Show an outer direct question with an embedded question and its necessary question mark.

issues.quote: an imperative ... has no subject and no finite verb at all
issues.explanation: Canonical imperatives commonly omit an overt subject, but their base-form verb is not thereby a to-infinitive/non-finite fragment. Some imperatives have overt subjects: You stay here.
issues.proposed_correction: Explain imperative clause form and understood addressee; distinguish imperative base forms from non-finite infinitival clauses.

issues.quote: a permanent truth ... should stay in the present
issues.explanation: Backshift can report a continuing truth without asserting that it ceased to be true. A present form often foregrounds continuing validity, but the past is not universally wrong.
issues.proposed_correction: Present both choices and their viewpoint; remove must/should never-backshift assertions.

issues.quote: The teacher ordered the students that they should stand up.
issues.explanation: Order supports content-clause constructions; a to-infinitive is often the simpler choice but a mandative that-clause is not universally ungrammatical.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach order + object + to and order + that-clause, with regional/register notes. Ask learners to rewrite in a specified pattern rather than mark every alternative as an error.

issues.quote: He requested to submit his documents earlier ... → ... his documents be submitted
issues.explanation: The rewrite changes the understood agent: requesting permission to submit oneself is different from requesting someone else to submit documents. Original request + to-infinitive also requires lexical/register checking rather than a blanket ban.
issues.proposed_correction: Specify who must submit and use He asked to submit his documents earlier or He requested that the office submit..., with agency preserved.

issues.quote: Report: I am busy today, he said.
issues.explanation: At least He said he is busy today and He said he was busy today can be legitimate same-day reports. No report time is specified.
issues.proposed_correction: Specify report made on a later day with conventional backshift, or accept the contextually valid alternatives.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: He said that he ____ finish the work by Friday.
issues.explanation: Will, would and can can all form grammatical reported clauses in suitable contexts; no original utterance or reporting time fixes a unique answer.
issues.proposed_correction: Supply original will and a later reporting context, or ask explicitly for the conventional backshift of will.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: She said that she ____ the file the previous day.
issues.explanation: Submitted and had submitted are both possible narrative choices; no direct original or mandated tense transformation establishes a unique answer.
issues.proposed_correction: Specify an exercise in backshifting an original past simple or supply a context requiring temporal disambiguation.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: You must submit it today. → He said that I ____ submit it that day.
issues.explanation: Must can remain in reported obligations, while had to is a common backshift. The key excludes a defensible retained modal without context.
issues.proposed_correction: Specify an expired obligation reported later, or discuss both must and had to.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: The witness said that he had seen the accused here the previous evening.
issues.explanation: Here is correct if the report is made at that location. The explanation supplies an elsewhere condition absent from the question.
issues.proposed_correction: State that reporting occurs elsewhere or add no error.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: wish itself is not further backshifted
issues.explanation: The keyed answer changes wish to wished. It is the embedded counterfactual past perfect that remains unchanged, not wish itself.
issues.proposed_correction: Identify wish → wished and had studied unchanged separately.

issues.quote: I never write that after ask.
issues.explanation: Ask may take a mandative content clause: She asked that the meeting be postponed. That is excluded before an embedded wh/if-question, not after ask in every construction.
issues.proposed_correction: Restrict the prohibition to reported interrogative patterns and teach ask + that for requests.

issues.quote: a/an — one of many, mentioned for the first time
issues.explanation: First mention is not identical to indefiniteness; the sun and a hearer-identifiable referent can take the on first mention, and a later new member can still take a. Singular generic the/a and role/institution zero uses also prevent the recap from being universal.
issues.proposed_correction: Base articles on countability and identifiability in context; teach generic alternatives, specificity versus definiteness, and title/role/institution exceptions.

issues.quote: a UN resolution ... pronounced as words
issues.explanation: UN is normally an initialism pronounced letter by letter, unlike NATO; a is right because U begins /j/.
issues.proposed_correction: Correct the pronunciation explanation without changing the article.

issues.quote: Made specific by what follows: the policy that was announced in May.
issues.explanation: A postmodifier does not mechanically force the: a policy that was announced in May is grammatical and may refer to one among several. Specificity is not sufficient for definiteness.
issues.proposed_correction: Contrast a/the + identical relative modifier with explicit contexts in which a reader can/cannot identify a unique referent.

issues.quote: record high stays article-free as a fixed phrase
issues.explanation: The model itself says to a record high. The note contradicts the written example.
issues.proposed_correction: Explain the singular count noun high and its a; compare record-high adjective use if needed.

issues.quote: the Punjab, the Netherlands, the Sudan ... plural or descriptive names take the
issues.explanation: Punjab is not a plural name; Sudan normally appears without the in contemporary official English, while the Sudan is historically attested. The table conflates historical convention with a productive rule.
issues.proposed_correction: Give contemporary default forms plus historical/regional notes for the Punjab/the Sudan. Preserve the Netherlands as conventional.

issues.quote: If nothing ... narrowing ... the noun must stand alone.
issues.explanation: Generic reference can use a singular indefinite or definite: A tiger is a mammal; The tiger is endangered. General categories do not invariably require zero article.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach zero plural/mass generics alongside generic a and the, with meaning and usage differences.

issues.quote: Games take no article. Only musical instruments take the.
issues.explanation: Play violin is an established zero-article alternative, particularly in American usage and musical contexts. Definite games can also take the when independently identified.
issues.proposed_correction: Use the violin as the British editorial default, explicitly accept play violin, and avoid only/all article claims.

issues.quote: Teachers are one of the most respected professions in society.
issues.explanation: The corrected model compares people with professions and fails the course's own like-with-like requirement.
issues.proposed_correction: Use Teaching is one of the most respected professions, or Teachers belong to one of the most respected professions.

issues.quote: He waited for ____ hour outside ____ office.
issues.explanation: An ... an is also grammatical when the office is unidentified; the supplied answer assumes a particular office without context.
issues.proposed_correction: Name a previously identified office in a preceding sentence.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: ____ is essential for economic growth.
issues.explanation: An education can be grammatical in a countable interpretation; the broad stem does not itself exclude that reading.
issues.proposed_correction: Ask for a general mass-noun reading or revise the alternatives/context so only the intended meaning fits.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: released from ____ prison after ____ appeal succeeded
issues.explanation: From prison and from the prison can both describe release of an inmate, depending on whether institutional state or identified establishment is foregrounded. The appeal context is also underspecified.
issues.proposed_correction: Specify institutional-state reading and prior identification, or accept both alternatives.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: an honour to serve on ____ committee that drafted the policy
issues.explanation: Both a committee that drafted the policy and the committee that drafted the policy are possible; uniqueness is not supplied by the relative clause alone.
issues.proposed_correction: Introduce a uniquely identified committee earlier, or ask what meaning the two articles convey.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: The unemployment among young graduates has risen sharply since 2019.
issues.explanation: The among-phrase can delimit a particular unemployment problem; definite article use is context-sensitive. It is not an unambiguous article error.
issues.proposed_correction: Provide a context establishing generic mass reference or use a less debatable article misuse.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: The report ____ was submitted last month ... [the … a]
issues.explanation: Every offered first gap is an article after an already determined report; the key yields The report the was submitted last month. The explanation describes a different question.
issues.proposed_correction: Replace first gap with a relative pronoun and update options/key, or remove the first The report and ask articles in two noun phrases. Validate rendered text after substitution.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: He was admitted to the hospital as a patient ...
issues.explanation: The hospital is normal American English and can also refer to a specific hospital. The question marks a legitimate standard variant as an error without limiting convention.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach to hospital as the British default and to the hospital as the American default; assess the distinction rather than rejecting the variant.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: education ... needs an urgent reform → ... urgent reform
issues.explanation: Reform has countable as well as mass uses. An urgent reform can denote a particular reform measure; the correction should not imply categorical uncountability. Definiteness of education also depends on context.
issues.proposed_correction: Accept singular countable reform where intended or specify broad systemic reform; explain both senses.

issues.quote: A pronoun must have exactly one possible antecedent.
issues.explanation: Pronouns can refer deictically, cataphorically, generically, to discourse propositions, or be dummy subjects. They do not all replace a previously named noun.
issues.proposed_correction: Distinguish reference types and actual ambiguous interpretation from legitimate discourse reference. Keep a clarity strategy rather than a universal syntactic law.

issues.quote: He performed better ... than ____ [me / I did]
issues.explanation: Than me is standard; than I did is a more explicit finite-clause alternative. Both offered answers fit.
issues.proposed_correction: Ask explicitly for the finite-clause version or allow both; explain that than can take an object pronoun.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: whom remains required ... in relative clauses in exam-standard prose
issues.explanation: Object who is standard in relative clauses. The question offers both who and whom without specifying a narrow formal convention. No authentic exam evidence supports the additional rule.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach whom as a formal option, especially directly following a preposition; accept object who and use a precise register instruction where a particular form is required.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: Themself is not a standard English word
issues.explanation: The form has established historical and contemporary uses. Authorities differ in labelling: Cambridge marks it not standard; Merriam-Webster records increasing use as a singular-they alternative. Non-existent/non-word claims are false, and standardness requires a stated editorial policy.
issues.proposed_correction: Use themselves as the course default; explain the recognised themself alternative and differing style policies without declaring the form nonexistent.

issues.location: rules[2]; examples[5]; d14q3; d14q12; d14c1; d14c6
issues.quote: A collective noun takes it and its, not they and their
issues.explanation: British notional plural agreement permits collective they/their, including a group acting in concert; the rule cannot be reduced to a universal singular requirement.
issues.proposed_correction: Present the committee has/its and the committee have/their as context/region-sensitive patterns and maintain intended notional agreement. Do not regrade older singular choices as mastery evidence.

issues.quote: Neither ... has submitted their affidavits [excluded]
issues.explanation: Singular they is explicitly accepted elsewhere in the same lesson; the key then requires his, making an inclusive alternative wrong. Neither of + plural can also take plural agreement informally.
issues.proposed_correction: Keep singular verb in formal editorial examples but accept singular they; specify one affidavit each if distributive number matters.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: A pronoun cannot refer to a possessive
issues.explanation: No general grammar constraint prevents reference to a person introduced in a possessive noun phrase. In Iqbal's poetry, he argues... can have a clear discourse interpretation.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach this as a possible clarity revision, not an absolute ban. Replace the scored item with genuinely ambiguous competing antecedents.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: This shows ... — this what?
issues.explanation: Demonstrative this may clearly refer to a proposition/event in preceding discourse. The audit-delay example with This is unacceptable has an obvious propositional referent.
issues.proposed_correction: Ask which version names the referent most explicitly, or accept clear propositional reference; distinguish style guidance from error correction.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: The commission published its findings, but they have not yet been acted upon ...
issues.explanation: They naturally refers to plural findings, reinforced by passive acted upon. Replacing it with these is an optional clarity/style choice, not a grammatical repair.
issues.proposed_correction: Label both versions acceptable and explain discourse focus; use a real referential ambiguity as a correction exercise.

issues.quote: each other for exactly two and one another for more than two
issues.explanation: Both reciprocal pronouns normally occur with groups of two or more. Both first and second options explicitly name two officers and are grammatical.
issues.proposed_correction: Accept both and explain modern usage; if asking group size, assess the noun phrase two officers rather than impose a fictitious pronoun distinction.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: did not accept the posting, which surprised everybody
issues.explanation: Sentential which can refer to the entire preceding refusal; this is a normal non-defining relative construction, not a missing antecedent.
issues.proposed_correction: Retain which as valid and offer his refusal as a stylistic explicit alternative.

issues.location: rules[0]; examples[0]; d15w1; d15q10; d15c2; d15c6; recap
issues.quote: Place only immediately before the word it limits.
issues.explanation: Normal mid-position only can focus a later object or adjunct. He only attempted two questions can mean he attempted just two. The lesson mistakes a clarity heuristic for a rigid scope rule, creating multiple-answer/error-free items.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach focus, context and prosody; recommend adjacency where needed for clarity but recognise ordinary mid-position. Rewrite scored questions to establish intended contrast.

issues.quote: He also signed ... means someone else signed it as well
issues.explanation: The same position can add another action by him, another signer, or another related proposition, depending on context. Position alone does not uniquely fix focus.
issues.proposed_correction: Use an explicit preceding sentence and contrasting readings; assess contextual interpretation.

issues.quote: A passive main clause almost always creates a dangler.
issues.explanation: Passive main clauses can have perfectly aligned participial adjuncts: Having been delayed, the project was launched. The lesson itself uses a correct passive model in d15c5. Reduced clauses can have passive rather than agentive subject relations.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach subject interpretation, not a passive ban. Give paired active/passive examples with both good and bad attachment.

issues.location: rules[3].plain and points[3,6]; examples[3]; d15w3; d15q9; checklist[3]
issues.quote: Absolute adjectives ... cannot take more, most, very or any other degree marker
issues.explanation: Gradability depends on sense and context. Unique meaning unusual can take degree modifiers; complete can mean more comprehensive; figurative very wooden is ordinary for acting. Even non-gradable senses take appropriate intensifiers (absolutely perfect).
issues.proposed_correction: Teach sense-dependent gradability and suitable intensifiers. State the course's formal style preference for unique meaning one-of-a-kind, rather than marking all graded uses ungrammatical.

issues.quote: Which sentence places the modifier correctly? ... almost released all / released almost all
issues.explanation: Both A and B are grammatical but make different claims. The stem supplies no intended quantity-versus-event meaning.
issues.proposed_correction: Specify funds are mostly released but some remain, or ask learners to explain both readings.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: Which sentence is unambiguous? ... Often students who study succeed.
issues.explanation: The third option is a possible sentence-initial frequency adverb and is not the medial squinting construction the question is trying to contrast. It can be at least as clear as the keyed A.
issues.proposed_correction: Replace C with a genuinely ambiguous construction or ask which sentence distinguishes regular study from frequent success using context.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: The minister ____ been criticised ... has repeatedly / repeatedly has
issues.explanation: Both has repeatedly been criticised and repeatedly has been criticised are grammatical; the latter is marked/emphatic but not wrong.
issues.proposed_correction: Ask for the neutral mid-position rather than the only grammatical position, or accept both.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: The scheme, after several years ... into its finances, was finally abandoned.
issues.explanation: The insertion is correctly paired and the subject agrees with its verb. Length may warrant editing but is not a grammatical fault. No no-error choice exists.
issues.proposed_correction: Add no error, or ask an unscored clarity revision while retaining the original as grammatical.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: Having failed ... the department cancelled the contract / minister almost promised / explained briefly
issues.explanation: Models infer a doer or intended scope without context. The contract deadline may be missed by a contractor; almost promising is a valid claim; explained briefly is grammatical and a long object can follow its recipient. These rewrites can change meaning or simply express a stylistic preference.
issues.proposed_correction: Supply intended agency/scope explicitly, preserve valid alternative readings, and label word-order revisions as stylistic where appropriate.

issues.quote: Prepositions cannot be reasoned out ... never an infinitive
issues.explanation: Prepositions have productive spatial/temporal/abstract meanings as well as lexical dependencies; complement possibilities extend beyond nouns and -ing, including finite interrogatives and specialised except/but infinitival constructions.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach productive semantics and lexical patterns together. Qualify the prepositional-to versus infinitival-to diagnostic and identify relevant complement exceptions.

issues.quote: fixed for 10 a.m. ... note: at a point
issues.explanation: The model uses for 10 a.m., not at. Its explanatory note does not match the actual word used.
issues.proposed_correction: Use begins at 10 a.m. or explain fixed for as a separate scheduling construction.

issues.quote: His approach is different than mine. [wrong]
issues.explanation: Different than is an established American alternative; different to also occurs in British English. A British default does not justify a universal wrong label.
issues.proposed_correction: Use different from as editorial default; mark different than as standard American and discuss British before-clause use.

issues.quote: Never add a preposition to ... enter
issues.explanation: Enter into has established senses (enter into an agreement/discussion) and enter can have prepositional complements depending on meaning. The blanket wording overgeneralises a sound beginner correction for enter the hall.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach each verb sense and complement pattern, distinguishing direct entry to a place from enter into negotiations.

issues.quote: confident about his ability [wrong]
issues.explanation: Confident about his ability is idiomatic and overlaps confident of/in; the imposed capability-versus-general-situation distinction is unsupported and too rigid. Angry at a person is also ordinary.
issues.proposed_correction: Provide typical preferences and meaning contrasts without declaring established overlapping prepositions universally wrong.

issues.quote: a phrasal verb ... is only out of register for the formal essay
issues.explanation: Many multi-word verbs occur naturally in formal writing (carry out, result in, account for). The final model itself recognises fairly formal uses.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach register item by item and choose exact meaning; avoid banning a structural category from formal prose.

issues.quote: no easy solution ____ the energy crisis [for / to]
issues.explanation: Solution for the energy crisis is a legitimate alternative to solution to; the stem cannot guarantee the unique key.
issues.proposed_correction: Use a truly constrained collocation or compare meaning/use rather than mark for wrong.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: to + infinitive after ... used to (habit)
issues.explanation: Used to for a past habit does take a base infinitive; be used to meaning accustomed takes -ing. This pitfall contradicts the lesson's own accurate examples.
issues.proposed_correction: Replace habit with accustomed and retain the contrasted used to work / is used to working patterns.

issues.quote: congratulated him for his success → ... on his success
issues.explanation: Congratulate on is a common neutral collocation, but congratulate for is established for an action/achievement and is not invariably wrong.
issues.proposed_correction: Keep on as the default recommendation while qualifying for and assess the genuine insist for/indifferent with faults separately.

issues.quote: Add ten entries a day ... by Day 30 ... three hundred
issues.explanation: Beginning on Day 16 provides 15 course days inclusive, hence 150 entries, not 300. The output target also prioritises a fixed quota over useful selection.
issues.proposed_correction: Use 150 if studying Days 16–30, or recommend a manageable number of genuinely useful collocations without an inflated total.

issues.quote: Both, same meaning: ... like, love, hate, prefer
issues.explanation: These verbs can take both forms, but choices often alter emphasis (activity enjoyment versus habitual preference/result). The same-meaning heading suppresses taught semantic distinctions.
issues.proposed_correction: Explain typical overlap and subtle differences, and would like/love/prefer restrictions.

issues.quote: The single exception ... passive of make restores to
issues.explanation: Perception verbs also take to-infinitives in passives: He was seen to leave; she was heard to say. Make is not the sole pattern.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach passive make/see/hear patterns with lexical limitations; distinguish passive let substitutions.

issues.quote: Collecting evidence, interviewing witnesses and drafting the report takes weeks, not take
issues.explanation: A coordination of three activities can take plural agreement; singular agreement is possible when conceptualised as one integrated process. The universal excludes an ordinary reading.
issues.proposed_correction: Present take as normal for separate coordinated activities and takes only when one integrated procedure is intended, with clear contexts.

issues.quote: We objected to him leaving the meeting ... [error]
issues.explanation: Accusative subjects of -ing clauses occur in standard English, including formal contexts. A possessive can foreground the event, but him is not an unconditional grammar error.
issues.proposed_correction: Accept both him/his with explanation of register/emphasis; if practising a named editorial convention, state it explicitly.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: a participle always borrows the subject of the main clause
issues.explanation: Absolute constructions can have their own subjects (Weather permitting, ...); trailing result clauses and supplement interpretations need broader analysis. Present/past participles are also not invariably active/passive (being examined; fallen leaves).
issues.proposed_correction: Teach the usual understood-subject pattern first, then absolute constructions, passive -ing forms, and non-passive past participial adjectives.

issues.quote: Finding out the fraud, the manager was suspended ... → ... head office suspended
issues.explanation: The original can mean the manager discovered fraud and was then suspended, e.g. retaliation. Passive voice does not itself create a dangler. The rewrite changes who discovered the fraud without evidence.
issues.proposed_correction: Supply a scenario identifying the discoverer, or use an unmistakably incompatible subject; preserve intended agency.

issues.quote: I regret ____ you that your application has been rejected [informing / to inform]
issues.explanation: Regret informing can refer to a prior disclosure; regret to inform can introduce the disclosure now. The stem lacks the time/context that distinguishes them.
issues.proposed_correction: Specify This is the first notice of the decision, or assess the two meanings directly.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: Use the comparative for two, the superlative for three or more
issues.explanation: This is a useful traditional formal convention, not an absolute grammatical restriction. Standard informal usage permits best/tallest of two. More/most is also not a universally interchangeable fallback for every two-syllable adjective.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach the formal default and recognised informal alternative; treat forms lexically and verify doubtful comparative spellings.

issues.quote: This is one of the better essays I have read this year. [wrong]
issues.explanation: One of the better essays is grammatical and means among the comparatively good essays; best makes a stronger claim. The fixed-superlative assertion is false.
issues.proposed_correction: Contrast the two valid meanings; retain one of + plural noun and correct agreement without forcing a superlative.

issues.quote: Lahore is older than ____ city in the province [any other / some other]
issues.explanation: Some other gives a weaker but grammatical comparison, whereas any other makes a superlative-like factual claim. The stem does not specify the intended strength.
issues.proposed_correction: Provide a stated ranking or ask which expression excludes Lahore while claiming greater age than every rival. Avoid unverified factual city-age rankings.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: Senior takes to and has no comparative form.
issues.explanation: Senior is gradable in modern standard use: more senior, most senior and senior enough appear in Oxford. More senior than me is a legitimate comparative alternative to senior to me.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach senior to and more senior than as established patterns; remove no-comparative and no-more assertions.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: Unique is absolute and takes no degree marker.
issues.explanation: The contextual unusual/rare sense can be graded in standard English. Unqualified scoring repeats the Day 15 defect.
issues.proposed_correction: State the intended one-of-a-kind sense or convert into a meaning/register comparison.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: Each of the provinces have submitted their own education plan.
issues.explanation: Under the lesson's own prescribed singular interpretation, both verb B and pronoun C are treated as faults; a one-segment answer does not cover the complete correction. Plural notional pronouns need context.
issues.proposed_correction: Target one unambiguous error or allow selection of all required changes; explain the distributive pronoun choice separately.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: Use rather than only with verbs
issues.explanation: Rather than can coordinate nouns and other structures, e.g. tea rather than coffee. Its distribution is not restricted to verbs.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach prefer X to Y and would prefer X rather than Y with suitable complete patterns, without banning noun comparisons.

issues.quote: funds ... treated as an uncountable amount of money
issues.explanation: Funds is a plural noun even when money is the intended aggregate; less funds and fewer funds can differ in interpretation/register. Calling the form uncountable conceals rather than explains the construction.
issues.proposed_correction: Use less money for an unambiguous mass/count contrast, and discuss aggregate quantity separately.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: inform takes of before a thing
issues.explanation: Inform about is also grammatical, and singular they may preserve a person-neutral reference. The model can be a valid rewrite without every changed form being compulsory.
issues.proposed_correction: Identify candidates/has as the required fixes; preserve valid informed about and singular their alternatives where intended.

issues.quote: The unemployment rate of Sindh is higher ... and it has fewer job opportunities
issues.explanation: The corrected model leaves it grammatically referring most directly to the unemployment rate, which cannot have job opportunities. The intended referent is Sindh.
issues.proposed_correction: Write ... and Sindh has fewer job opportunities..., keeping the comparison scope explicit.

issues.quote: comma before ... never a semicolon and never nothing
issues.explanation: A comma can be omitted between very short coordinated independent clauses; semicolons before coordinating conjunctions can separate long/complex clauses. A style default is presented as an exceptionless syntax rule.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach the usual comma pattern plus short-clause and complex-clause style variation; preserve sentence boundaries.

issues.quote: Preposition + noun: in order to, so as to
issues.explanation: These introduce infinitival purpose constructions, not noun complements. The category heading contradicts the structures.
issues.proposed_correction: Give a separate infinitival purpose column; distinguish for + noun/-ing where relevant.

issues.quote: Due to ... needs a form of be before it
issues.explanation: Contemporary due to also introduces an adjunct reason phrase without be. The question's correct was due to supplies the missing finite verb, but the explanation falsely bans due to elsewhere.
issues.proposed_correction: Explain the actual clause needs a finite predicate here and qualify the historical adjectival-only style preference.

issues.quote: Notwithstanding takes a noun phrase, not a clause
issues.explanation: Notwithstanding is also a conjunction meaning although, including with a finite clause and without that; Merriam-Webster explicitly exemplifies that construction.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach the less common formal conjunctive use; do not mark the finite clause ungrammatical. Replace the scored item or include no error.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: not only with but also [each pair is fixed]
issues.explanation: Also can be omitted in the not only ... but pattern, as Cambridge explains. Complete parallelism also concerns compatible syntactic functions rather than an absolute identity of word classes.
issues.proposed_correction: Show optional also and distinguish shared function from identical form; avoid overcorrecting accepted coordination.

issues.quote: arbitrary and without lawful authority ... two adjective phrases
issues.explanation: Without lawful authority is a prepositional phrase, functioning as a predicative complement alongside the adjective arbitrary. The example is valid but its analysis is wrong and contradicts the identical-form rule.
issues.proposed_correction: Label adjective phrase + prepositional phrase with compatible predicative functions; use this to explain limits of surface-form parallelism.

issues.quote: As the rains failed, so the wheat output fell ... [error]
issues.explanation: As ... so is an established correlative pattern, particularly proportional or emphatic constructions; a general ban is unsafe. Whether this specific causal example is stylistically preferred requires interpretation.
issues.proposed_correction: Use a clearly redundant because ... so exercise under an explicit standard convention, or teach as/so correlatives separately. Do not rely on the blanket one-connector law.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: reduced the syllabus; ... increased number of papers [however / moreover]
issues.explanation: A contrast is plausible, but moreover can legitimately add a second fact, and a policy could link them causally. Context does not uniquely establish the intended logical relation.
issues.proposed_correction: State that the second development is unexpected despite reduced coverage, or ask learners to explain how connector choice changes the implied relationship.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: Balochistan's revenue is smaller than what Punjab collects. [wrong]
issues.explanation: What Punjab collects is a fused relative/nominal construction denoting the amount collected. It can serve as the comparison term. Comparisons routinely take finite clauses; noun-versus-clause alone does not invalidate them.
issues.proposed_correction: Accept the sentence and explain its implicit amount interpretation; teach a genuine category mismatch such as revenue versus Punjab itself.

issues.quote: As ... as needs the same clause shape on both sides
issues.explanation: Comparative clauses need semantic comparability, not identical surface clause shape. The original poor-monitoring/generous-funding comparison may be rhetorically awkward, but its clause shape is not inherently ungrammatical.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach comparative clause structure and ellipsis. Frame the suggested rewrite as rhetorical parallelism, distinct from grammatical correction.

issues.quote: Choose one form ... either repeat to before every item or use it only once
issues.explanation: Mixed category coordination can be grammatical when functions match; repetition of to/prepositions is not universally all-or-none, and voice can change for discourse reasons. The checklist overgeneralises a useful editing heuristic.
issues.proposed_correction: Teach uniform form as a clarity default, illustrate compatible unlike categories and shared/partial ellipsis, and distinguish errors from style recommendations.

issues.quote: The board is examining efficiency, transparency and being accountable.
issues.explanation: A gerund-participial clause can occupy a nominal complement function alongside noun phrases. This may be less parallel rhetorically but is not automatically a syntactic error. Likewise d20q5 can coordinate a first clause with a second clause.
issues.proposed_correction: Ask for the most rhetorically parallel rewrite, or use a complement form the governing verb actually excludes. Keep objective grammar error detection unambiguous.

issues.quote: To draft a summary is harder than drafting a note. [excluded]
issues.explanation: A mixed to-infinitival/-ing comparison can be grammatical; matching forms is the more symmetrical rhetorical choice, not a categorical requirement.
issues.proposed_correction: Keep the question explicitly about matching surface form, and explain that the alternative may remain grammatical rather than label it incorrect.
issues.legacy_answer_policy: retain historical response and authored version; do not silently regrade

issues.quote: Which sentence keeps voice consistent?
issues.explanation: The question is answerable as a style-pattern identification, but other options with active/passive shifts are grammatical and can improve information flow. A proficiency report should not count them as grammar failures.
issues.proposed_correction: Tag this as style/organisation recognition; explain the discourse reasons for choosing a voice and avoid a general voice-consistency prohibition.

issues.quote: Recommend takes gerunds, so all three items become gerunds
issues.explanation: Recommend also takes mandative that-clauses and object-dependent patterns. The model is a good parallel rewrite, but the explanation overstates lexical exclusivity.
issues.proposed_correction: Say gerunds are one valid repeated pattern; give a parallel set of that-clauses as another solution.
